Coverage from The Economic Times on MSN: "How 90 Claude Opus 5.5 agents found a 27-year-old compound in 3 days to solve computing's heat problem"
More than 90 Claude Opus 5.5 agents spent three days searching for materials that could enable cooler spin-based computing. They identified two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates; ...

Coverage from ZDNet: "Claude Opus 5.5 delivers Fable 5.1 performance – and costs 40% less"
Less than two months after the release of Claude Opus 5, Anthropic is back with Opus 5.5. The big pitch for Opus 5 was that it had “near Fable” performance at half the price. This time, the headline is that the workhorse AI Opus 5.5 delivers Fable 5.1 performance for most work and costs about 40% less to run.
“Our customers use Box AI on enormous amounts of content, so speed and cost are a top priority,” Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products at Box, reports. “In our evaluations, Claude Opus 5.5 used a third of the tokens Opus 5 did, and its answers were 40% less verbose without losing accuracy. We expect that to matter a lot for teams running agents across their content in areas like financial services and the public sector.”
Anthropic says that, “Over the coming weeks, we’ll also be launching Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.” Opus 5.5 is available today.
I’ve been using the heck out of Claude Code with Opus 5, so I’m particularly hopeful that the company’s performance claims are accurate. The company says it “generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.”
Also: Anthropic merges Claude chat and Cowork into one
Token prices and subscription plans are addressed in today’s announcement . Tokens are priced at 20% less than when used with Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also reportedly “needs fewer tokens for higher quality work.”
For subscription users like me, Anthropic is raising its five-hour usage limits by 20%. That’s basically a 20% bigger gas tank for how much AI chomping you can use during five hours. While my Max plan doesn’t get reset often, it does get reset. For those on $20/month plans, this could be a considerable win. On top of that, the company says that both 5-hour and weekly usage limits go further because Opus 5.5 costs less than Opus 5.
These seem to be additive. There’s a 20% larger bucket coupled with a 25% slower burn, meaning that effective usage seems to be about a 50% greater run capacity with Opus 5.5. That’s not an inconsiderable quality-of-life improvement.
Anthropic also says that Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally than prior models. If it’s even just a little less obsequious, I’d be happy. Sometimes, Opus can be a total suck-up, particularly when it’s done something wrong.
Also: The AI models that cheat the most, according to new CAIS benchmark
“Verbose, hard-to-follow output has been my biggest frustration with frontier models, and Claude Opus 5.5 fixes it,” says John Ruelas, staff software engineer at Ramp.

Background (Spintronics, Wikipedia):
Spintronics, also known as spin electronics, is the study of the intrinsic spin of the electron and its associated magnetic moment, in addition to its fundamental electronic charge, in solid-state devices. The field of spintronics concerns spin-charge coupling in metallic systems. The analogous effects in insulators fall into the field of multiferroics.

Background (Magnetic semiconductor, Wikipedia):
Magnetic semiconductors are semiconductor materials that exhibit both ferromagnetism and useful semiconductor properties. If implemented in devices, these materials could provide a new type of control of conduction. Whereas traditional electronics are based on control of charge carriers, practical magnetic semiconductors would also allow control of quantum spin state. This would theoretically provide near-total spin polarization, which is an important property for spintronics applications, e.g. spin transistors.

text:
Ninety AI agents spent three days sorting through decades of research.

They found two materials that solve a fundamental computing heat problem nobody else could crack.

That speed is the whole story.

Researchers have long chased materials that sort electrons by spin while their magnetism cancels out.

It is the key requirement for spintronics, a field that could make microchips run without generating heat.

The team deployed more than 90 Claude Opus 5.5 agents to run simulations.

In three days, the software identified two room temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates: YBaMnFeO5 and KV[Cr(CN)6].

The search was not theoretical. It used real material chemistry to narrow down decades of dead ends.

The discovery highlights a quiet shift in how science gets done.
• 90+ agents deployed in parallel
• 3 days of simulation run time
• 2 viable candidates uncovered

My read: the most valuable use of frontier AI will not be writing emails or generating images. It will be brute-forcing materials science problems that take human researchers a lifetime to test.

The catch is real. These are simulation candidates, not experimentally verified compounds sitting in a lab.

Would you trust a material found by software to build the next generation of microchips?

Source: @valsai on X, with reporting from The Economic Times on MSN and ZDNet
alt_openings:
1. Shape: Bare number first
Line 1: 90 AI agents just did three years of materials research in 72 hours.
Line 2: They found two physical compounds that could solve computing's heat problem.
Prefer when: The scale of the agent swarm is the most startling fact in the material.

2. Shape: Corrective
Line 1: Finding new semiconductor materials does not require decades of lab work anymore.
Line 2: A team let autonomous software loose on the problem and found two candidates in three days.
Prefer when: You want to directly challenge the reader's assumption about how long R&D takes.

3. Shape: Your X
Line 1: Your next microchip may be built from a material discovered by software in a weekend.
Line 2: Autonomous agents just simulated and found two room-temperature magnetic semiconductors in three days.
Prefer when: You want to tie an abstract scientific breakthrough directly to the hardware the reader uses daily.

Pick: The opening with 90 AI agents because it immediately establishes the concrete scale and speed of the story without relying on jargon.
